title: Saudi Prince Found Dead in London Hotel After Drug Cocktail, Inquest Rules
excerpt: A London coroner has ruled the death of 29-year-old Prince Abdullah bin Fahad al-Saud as misadventure after toxicology revealed fatal levels of GHB and nearly three times the legal alcohol limit in his system.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Prince Abdullah bin Fahad al-Saud died from multi-drug ingestion at a London hotel on November 25, 2025.
  • Toxicology revealed fatal levels of GHB and nearly three times the legal alcohol limit in his system.
  • He had previously undergone detox treatment but missed follow-up appointments after discharge.
  • The coroner ruled his death as misadventure, with no evidence of suicide or foul play.
  • The case highlights substance abuse challenges among Gulf royals in London.

Prince Abdullah bin Fahad bin Abdullah bin Abdulaziz bin Jalawi al-Saud, a 29-year-old member of Saudi Arabia's ruling dynasty, died of multi-drug ingestion at a luxury London hotel last November, a coroner's inquest has concluded. Assistant Coroner Jean Harkin recorded a verdict of death by misadventure at Inner West London Coroner's Court.

The prince was discovered fully clothed on the bathroom floor of his £600-a-night room at the Marriott Hotel in Kensington on November 25, 2025. A cleaner who unlocked the door to his fifth-floor room found him unresponsive. Hotel security and paramedics were called but were unable to resuscitate him, and he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Toxicology Findings

A toxicology report presented to the court revealed a devastating combination of substances in the prince's system. His blood ethanol concentration stood at 222mg per 100ml of blood — nearly three times England's legal drink-drive limit of 80mg, and in a range that could by itself cause a coma, according to the report.

https://x.com/TheCradleMedia/status/2080594337931419729

More critically, the prince had potentially fatal levels of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a powerful depressant commonly used as a recreational drug. Tests also detected traces of cannabis, a recreational dose of the anti-anxiety medication Xanax, and other anti-anxiety medicines at therapeutic levels.

A post-mortem examination found no acute or chronic illnesses. The medical cause of death was recorded as cardiac arrest resulting from multi-drug ingestion.

History of Treatment and Struggle

The court heard that Prince Abdullah had been struggling with alcohol and prescription drug use in the months before his death. In August 2025, he was admitted to the Priory clinic in Roehampton, southwest London — a facility where stays can cost up to £35,000 a week — for detoxification from alcohol, benzodiazepines, and the anti-anxiety drug pregabalin.

"He was assessed as having symptoms of low mood and anxiety on admission. When he was discharged he was considered not to be at risk of suicide. He engaged well and completed his treatment."

— Dr Victoria Chamorro, Consultant Psychiatrist

After leaving the Priory, Prince Abdullah underwent further treatment at the private Rainford Hall clinic in St Helens, Merseyside, where weekly stays cost around £7,000. He was also diagnosed with an upper respiratory tract infection during this stay. He recovered and left the facility on October 14, 2025 — just five weeks before his death.

According to Dr Chamorro, the prince had been discharged with a friend but subsequently failed to attend scheduled follow-up appointments via Zoom. "Nevertheless there was no concern for him," she told the court, according to The Times.

The prince checked into the Marriott Hotel on November 19 for a planned one-week stay. CCTV footage showed him going outside to smoke a cigarette the evening before his death — the last time he was seen alive. The footage also confirmed he was alone that night, and the court found no evidence of third-party involvement.

Harkin told the court there was nothing to suggest the prince had intended to take his own life. No note was found in his room, and reports from both the Priory and Rainford Hall indicated no suicidal concerns, according to The Times.

"I would like to offer my sincere condolences to the family of Abdullah."

— Jean Harkin, Assistant Coroner

Royal Family Response

The Saudi Royal Court issued an official statement on December 2, 2025, a week after his death, announcing that "Prince Abdullah bin Fahd bin Abdullah bin Abdulaziz bin Musaid bin Jalawi Al Saud has passed away to the mercy of Almighty God, outside the Kingdom." A funeral prayer was held at the Imam Turki bin Abdullah Mosque in Riyadh, attended by a large number of princes and officials.

A source described Prince Abdullah to Taroudant Press as a "quiet and well-liked figure within the royal family," known for "discreet philanthropic contributions to societal projects."

What's Next

With the inquest concluded and the verdict of misadventure recorded, the case is now formally closed. No criminal investigation is expected. The case has, however, drawn renewed attention to the presence of Gulf royals in London and the challenges of substance abuse treatment — questions that resonate beyond national borders in a city that serves as a hub for expatriate communities from across South Asia and the Middle East.
nri_angle: The case draws attention to Gulf royal families' ties to London, a city home to hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin residents, and to broader questions about substance abuse among expatriate communities in the UK and the Gulf.
